title: A heritable body plan the ancestor never had

concept.text: The proposed innovation is the ability to specify a novel animal structure and engineer an animal that develops it, uses it and passes the capacity to build it to its offspring. An example would be an additional functional, innervated appendage or a new sensory structure integrated into the animal’s behavior. The target is a reproducible developmental outcome in a breeding lineage, rather than an anatomical alteration that must be surgically recreated in every individual. These functional and inheritance requirements are proposed here as a concrete milestone.

The broader ambition is an anatomical compiler: a way to translate a desired anatomical design into biological instructions that produce it. Jamie A. Davies and Michael Levin describe this goal in their January 2023 review of synthetic morphology, including the prospect of generating DNA instructions from a specified design. This supplies a research framework for the innovation; it does not establish that such a compiler has been built.

Conceptual clarification: novelty concerns the resulting structure or anatomical arrangement, not necessarily the invention of entirely new developmental machinery. A structure absent from the species and its documented natural variation might be built by redirecting, combining or redeploying ancestral programs. The title therefore describes a new anatomical outcome; it should not be read as requiring every component or developmental mechanism to lack an evolutionary antecedent.

significance.text: If achieved, the proposed milestone would make animal anatomy a more directly designable biological property. A successful intervention would connect a chosen anatomical specification to development, functional integration and inheritance. Davies and Levin’s anatomical-compiler goal provides the technical basis for this ambition, while their discussion of developmental plasticity explains why the space of possible outcomes may extend beyond familiar embryogenesis.

Conditional significance assessment: one breeding lineage with a specified, useful novel structure would establish a substantial capability in developmental engineering. Its immediate consequence would be a reproducible example of designing an inherited anatomical outcome. It would also create an experimental system for investigating how tissues coordinate growth, connections and behavior when the overall anatomy differs from the species-typical arrangement.

Conditional downstream possibilities include broader anatomical engineering and new approaches to tissue reconstruction or regenerative medicine. Those possibilities would require additional advances. One successful lineage would demonstrate one design, not a general compiler for arbitrary anatomy, predictable performance across species or reliable repair of human limbs. Functional novelty would also need to be assessed alongside survival, reproduction and costs to the rest of the animal.

The compiler analogy has a practical limit: a specification must be realized through interacting living tissues whose development and behavior require experimental validation. The supplied review identifies developmental knowledge gaps as constraints on bottom-up bioengineering. Its preview also describes the construction of new arrangements of living material, so the original categorical assertion that animal form cannot be composed is too broad. The consequential target here is the particular combination of specified novelty, functional integration and germline inheritance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is generative: starting with a defined anatomical outcome and identifying interventions that cause an animal to build it, integrate it into its functioning and transmit that developmental capacity through the germline. Davies and Levin’s January 2023 review identifies gaps in developmental knowledge as limitations on bottom-up bioengineering. That supports the underlying research problem, but the supplied historical preview does not establish the field’s complete capabilities or limitations as of November 2026.

Engineering analysis: a convincing solution would need to coordinate where a structure forms, which cells contribute, how growth and shape are controlled, and how the structure connects to the animal. Depending on the design, integration could require innervation, circulation, mechanical attachment or sensory processing. Producing recognizable anatomy alone would leave unresolved whether the structure works and whether it disrupts existing organs or behavior.

Engineering analysis: inheritance adds a separate barrier. A developmental intervention must be encoded or otherwise established in a germline-transmissible form, and offspring must reconstruct the intended anatomy without repeated surgical assembly. The resulting lineage must remain viable and fertile. Researchers would also need to distinguish reliable redevelopment of the intended design from variable malformations, ordinary variation and selection for unintended outcomes.

Scope clarification: a general anatomical compiler would require more than solving these problems once. It would need a dependable relationship between specifications, interventions and outcomes across multiple designs and biological contexts. No particular molecular mechanism is required by this concept: genetic regulation, synthetic circuits, bioelectric control and other developmental interventions are possible areas of overlap, but the supplied evidence does not establish which combination would suffice.

current_state.text: Davies and Levin’s review, “Synthetic morphology with agential materials,” was published on 19 January 2023 in Nature Reviews Bioengineering, volume 1, pages 46–59. Its accessible key points describe an anatomical compiler as a goal of synthetic morphology and identify missing developmental knowledge as a limitation on bottom-up approaches. These are documented statements about the research agenda at that date, rather than a report of a completed compiler.

The review’s accessible abstract discusses experimental embryology, including organoids and xenobots, as evidence that living materials can produce outcomes beyond familiar embryogenesis. This supports the narrower conclusion that tissues display developmental plasticity and can form new arrangements. The supplied preview does not provide enough experimental detail to establish the functional, reproductive or germline status of particular systems, or to determine whether any meets the proposed milestone.

The retained source is a subscription preview containing the abstract and key points; the substantive article body and figures were unavailable in the supplied review. The extraction was untruncated, but that does not make the underlying article fully accessible. Its bibliography is not evidence that the referenced experiments were inspected. Detailed claims about synthetic-circuit patterning, specific organ-building demonstrations or the absence of breeding lineages therefore cannot be established from this material alone.

Evidence boundary: no freshness search record or later experimental evidence was supplied. Consequently, the material does not establish whether a functional, complex, germline-heritable novel animal structure had been demonstrated by 1 November 2026, or whether a broader compiler remained unrealized then. This uncertainty limits the present-day assessment; it is not evidence that such demonstrations are false or impossible. The innovation remains a prospective target in this record.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: before experimentation, specify a defined anatomical structure or arrangement and the intervention intended to produce it in a laboratory vertebrate or complex invertebrate. Document why the outcome falls outside the species’ known natural variation, and define how it will be distinguished from an ordinary variant or nonspecific malformation. An additional functional appendage or a new sensory structure would be possible targets, rather than mandatory designs.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified anatomy and intervention distinguish novelty from variation or malformation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional requirements: show that the structure develops in the intended location and performs its specified role within the animal. For an appendage, this could include appropriate innervation and demonstrated use; for a sensory structure, it would require evidence that its input contributes to behavior. Suitable controls should distinguish the new structure’s contribution from compensation by existing anatomy. Survival and successful reproduction are required parts of the proposed milestone.
completion_criteria.label: Intended structure functions in animals that survive and reproduce

completion_criteria.text: Proposed inheritance and reproducibility requirements: breeding should establish germline transmission of the developmental capacity and redevelopment of the structure in offspring without repeated microsurgery. Report the frequency of the intended outcome, variation in form and function, fertility and adverse effects across generations. Independent replication would strengthen the claim. The supplied material establishes no accepted minimum number of animals or generations, so numerical thresholds would need to be justified for the chosen system.
completion_criteria.label: Germline transmission rebuilds offspring anatomy with multigenerational outcomes reported

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation rules: two-headed planarians, rearranged frog-cell xenobots or Hox-induced phenotypes should be judged against the same requirements rather than excluded solely by their labels. A result that is lethal, lacks demonstrated function or requires repeated physical reconstruction would fail the corresponding criterion. The supplied preview does not independently establish those properties for every example. A qualifying result would establish one designed heritable anatomy; finite tests across further designs would establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Common qualification criteria apply across examples without establishing literal universality

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison with ZOO-02, “Complete limb regeneration in an adult mammal”: both concern the control and integration of complex anatomy. Regeneration targets restoration of a species-typical structure, whereas ZOO-09 targets a specified new anatomical outcome that is inherited. They may nevertheless reuse the same ancestral developmental programs. Explaining the function of an existing unusual structure is another distinct task: it does not itself demonstrate the engineering of heritable anatomical novelty.

Roster-based comparison with ZOO-01, “A fertile animal booted from a chemically synthesized genome,” and ZOO-10, “Fertile adulthood from a vertebrate cell line, with no gestational parent”: all involve development and reproductive competence. Their stated milestones concern genome construction or the route from cells to adulthood. Neither title requires novel anatomy, while ZOO-09 does not require a wholly synthesized genome or development without a gestational parent.

Roster-based comparison with ZOO-06, “A germline-transmitted photosynthetic organelle in an animal,” and ZOO-08, “Experimental origin of animal multicellular development”: ZOO-06 shares the challenge of integrating and inheriting a new biological capability, but its target is an organelle rather than a novel macroscopic structure. ZOO-08 concerns the origin of multicellular development, whereas ZOO-09 concerns directing an animal’s development toward a specified anatomical novelty. Success on one would not automatically complete the other.

Roster-based comparison with ZOO-03, “Negligible senescence as an installed life-history program,” ZOO-04, “Self-sustaining populations reconstructed from extinct animal species,” and ZOO-07, “Reversible whole-animal biostasis”: these address aging, population reconstruction and reversible preservation, respectively. They could share enabling methods in genetics, reproduction or whole-animal physiology with ZOO-09, but their stated outcomes do not require a new inherited anatomical arrangement. Reconstructing an extinct anatomy also differs from specifying an anatomical outcome absent from the target species.

Roster-based comparison with ZOO-05, “Two-way semantic communication with another animal species”: a new sensory structure could intersect with communication research, but anatomical function would not by itself demonstrate semantic exchange. Conversely, semantic communication need not require anatomical modification. These comparisons use the supplied roster titles; detailed evidence or completion criteria for the other entries were not supplied.

unresolved_issues: Whether any demonstration by 1 November 2026 satisfies the proposed combination of specified anatomical novelty, functional integration, fertility and germline redevelopment remains unresolved.

The supplied preview does not establish the detailed capabilities or limits of synthetic genetic circuits, or the reproductive and inheritance properties of particular organoid, xenobot, planarian or Hox experiments.

A chosen demonstration would need a defensible account of documented natural variation and the level at which anatomical novelty is claimed; absence from all evolutionary ancestors is not established.
Appropriate sample sizes, generation counts, acceptable variability, functional performance and adverse-effect boundaries remain to be proposed for a specific organism and design.
The relationship between a successful individual design and a reusable design method would require additional demonstrations across specified anatomical targets.
Detailed comparisons with other roster entries remain limited by the absence of their full concept and evidence records.

brief.title: New body parts that animals can pass to their young
possible: Researchers could design an animal with an extra working limb or a new sense, then breed offspring that develop the same structure. Each animal would grow it for itself, without surgery to assemble it.
why: Animal anatomy would become something researchers could deliberately design. A breeding lineage would also let biologists study how tissues coordinate growth, connections and behavior when the body has an unfamiliar shape.

sources.showed: Their review describes how living tissues can form new arrangements. It outlines the goal of translating a chosen body design into DNA instructions.
sources.quote: Synthetic bioengineering allows the construction of new arrangements of living material.
sources.cited_for: Living tissues can produce unfamiliar forms, providing a basis for designing anatomy.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate a designed, functional new structure that animals pass to their offspring.

sources.who: Georg Halder and colleagues at the University of Basel
sources.showed: They identified genes needed for an eye-building gene to induce extra eyes in fruit flies. This shows how existing developmental machinery can produce eyes in unusual places.
sources.quote:
We demonstrate that ey function
is required for the expression of so and eya in the eye disc.
sources.cited_for: Redirecting existing developmental programs can produce extra structures.
sources.not_established: Extra eye formation does not establish useful vision, successful reproduction or reliable rebuilding of the anatomy across generations.

sources.who: Markus Tögel, Günther Pass and Achim Paululat
sources.showed: They found extra working wing hearts in flies with extra wings. Wing hearts are small pumping organs that help wings mature.
sources.quote: We show that a second pair of functional wing hearts is formed in the transformed third thoracic segment and that all wing hearts originate from the wild-type population of wing heart progenitor cells.
sources.cited_for: An altered body arrangement can develop working supporting organs.
sources.not_established: Working wing hearts do not establish useful flight or a specified new anatomy reliably rebuilt in fertile offspring.

shown: Halder and colleagues traced genetic controls behind extra eyes in fruit flies. Tögel and colleagues found that flies with extra wings also develop working pumping organs to support them. These results show that existing body-building programs can produce altered anatomy.
missing: A qualifying demonstration would need a planned new structure that works in an animal that survives and reproduces.
Offspring would need to rebuild the structure through inherited biological instructions, without repeated surgical assembly.
Breeding would need to establish reliable form and function, fertility and effects on the rest of the animal.

milestones.label: A planned structure clearly exceeds ordinary variation
milestones.explanation: A design and intervention specified before experiments would have to produce anatomy beyond known variation in a lab animal with a backbone or a complex animal without one. This would distinguish intended novelty from malformation.

milestones.label: The structure works in animals that survive and reproduce
milestones.explanation: The structure would have to grow in its intended location and perform its role in animals that survive and reproduce, with controls confirming its contribution. This would establish useful integration into the body.

milestones.label: Offspring reliably rebuild the inherited structure
milestones.explanation: Breeding would have to show inherited rebuilding without repeated surgery, with form, function, frequency, fertility and adverse effects reported across generations. This would establish a reproducible inherited capacity.

milestones.label: The same criteria apply across different examples
milestones.explanation: Rearranged cells and animals with redirected body-building genes would have to meet the same criteria as other candidates. A qualifying result would establish a particular inherited design; further tests would establish breadth.

uncertain: Whether any animal already meets the full combination of planned novelty, useful function, fertility and inherited rebuilding remains unresolved.
What counts as novel anatomy, and how much variation or harm is acceptable, needs a defensible standard for each design.
A successful design may not yield a reusable method for designing other structures.

page.title: Synthetic morphology with germline inheritance
page.definition: An animal lineage develops a specified anatomical structure or arrangement outside the species’ documented natural variation, uses it in a demonstrated physiological or behavioral role, and transmits the capacity to construct it through sperm or eggs. Descendants rebuild the anatomy without surgical assembly.

goal.need: Constructing specified anatomy provides a test of developmental theories. The ectopic-eye experiments below distinguish organ formation from integration into learned behavior: producing a recognizable structure does not establish its functional use. Germline inheritance adds the requirement that descendants reconstruct the anatomical outcome.

figures.caption: Anatomical and behavioral outcomes in the 2013 Xenopus ectopic-eye study
rows: Learning with a trunk-innervating tail eye after removal of native eyes
figures.note: These are separate experimental cohorts, not successive stages measured in the same denominator. The anatomy was surgically transplanted; inheritance was not tested.

statements.body: Jamie A. Davies, University of Edinburgh, proposing synthetic morphology
statements.quote: with the aim of programming cells to organize themselves into specific, novel arrangements, structures and tissues.

statements.body: Jamie Davies and Michael Levin, University of Edinburgh and Tufts University
statements.quote: Synthetic morphology aims at creating an 'anatomical compiler' that writes DNA instructions based on a specific design goal
statements.context: The accepted manuscript states an anatomical-design goal without requiring germline inheritance.

completion.title: A breeding lineage reconstructs a specified novel anatomy that functions and permits reproduction.
completion.criterion: A structure or anatomical arrangement specified before intervention, and outside the species’ documented natural variation, develops without surgical assembly and performs its specified physiological or behavioral role. Sexual offspring inherit the developmental capacity, reconstruct the anatomy and demonstrate the same role. Those descendants themselves reproduce. All conditions must hold in the same lineage.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; operational test because no external qualification for this combined capability was found.
completion.basis: Searches for synthetic-morphology standards, anatomical-compiler benchmarks, roadmaps, prizes and germline-transmission protocols found no published combined qualification. Davies’s self-construction proposal and Davies and Levin’s compiler goal support specified anatomy, but neither establishes an inheritance test. This criterion covers one functional inherited anatomical design.

milestones.title: An animal develops a specified anatomical change without surgical assembly.
milestones.criterion: An intervention produces the specified structure or arrangement, with anatomical evidence establishing its identity and location. Halder and colleagues reported ectopic eyes on fly wings, legs and antennae on 24 March 1995. Their paper published online on 19 May 1998 reported extra eyes in nearly 100% of pharate adults, meaning adults still inside the pupal case; no denominator accompanied that percentage. These are demonstrations of redeployed eye development.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; no external general qualification for specified anatomical construction was found. The cited papers supply experimental evidence.

milestones.title: An altered anatomical structure performs its specified physiological or behavioral role.
milestones.criterion: Functional measurements establish that the altered structure contributes its specified role within the animal. Tögel and colleagues’ 2022 paper reports a second pair of functional wing hearts, small pumping organs, in four-winged flies. The cited abstract gives no animal count. This establishes coordinated development of additional functioning organs; it does not establish a prespecified anatomical design transmitted through a breeding lineage.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; no universal functional-integration qualification was found. The cited experiment concerns fly wing hearts.

milestones.title: Sexual offspring inherit and reconstruct the specified anatomical change without surgical assembly.
milestones.criterion: Offspring inherit the capacity to reconstruct the specified anatomy; inheriting a genetic marker alone does not meet this test. Pan and Rubin’s paper of 22 December 1998 reports five Four eyes mutant fly lines, with ectopic eyes in 20–80% of flies depending on the line. Animal denominators and generation counts were not supplied for those percentages. These lines provide evidence of inherited anatomical variation, but the paper does not test behavioral use of their ectopic eyes.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; no external qualification combining germline transmission with reconstruction of specified novel anatomy was found.

not_found: No published demonstration was found establishing prior anatomical specification, functional use, germline redevelopment and descendant fertility together in the same lineage.
No external minimum animal count, penetrance, generation count or acceptable adverse-effect boundary was found for this combined capability.

results.finding: Drosophila: nearly 100% of pharate adults developed extra eyes; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The 1998 paper reports induced extra eyes and identifies an extra eye on a leg in Figure 6. The percentage has no reported denominator.
results.quote:
Such animals readily induced ectopic
expression of so and eya (Fig. 5H,I,K,L) and nearly 100% of
pharate adult ﬂies developed extra eyes.

results.finding: Four-winged Ubx-mutant flies developed a second pair of wing hearts; animal count not stated.
results.detail: The additional organs formed in the transformed third thoracic segment. The source describes an existing mutant but does not report an intervention specifying the change.
results.quote: We show that a second pair of functional wing hearts is formed in the transformed third thoracic segment and that all wing hearts originate from the wild-type population of wing heart progenitor cells.

results.finding: Four-winged Ubx-mutant flies formed a second pair of functional wing hearts; animal count not stated.
results.detail: The abstract reports the additional hearts as functional but does not give the underlying functional measurements.
results.quote: We show that a second pair of functional wing hearts is formed in the transformed third thoracic segment and that all wing hearts originate from the wild-type population of wing heart progenitor cells.

results.finding: In 12 beetles with ectopic eyes and no regular eyes, 11 responded to light.
results.detail: The response was partially restored: beetles lowered their heads, turned around, or did both. None of 15 beetles without either set of eyes responded. Germline inheritance was not assessed.
results.quote:
We found that most
individuals possessing ectopic compound eyes but lacking regular
lateral compound eyes (B+I+) eventually reacted to the light stimulus
by either lowering their head or turning around or a combination
thereof (11/12) (Table S1 and Movie S1).

results.finding: F1 fruit flies from a transgenic cross developed ectopic eyes; specimen count was not reported.
results.detail: The authors selected F1 offspring with ectopic eyes for microscopy. They assisted the flies' emergence from the pupal case; the eyes were not surgically assembled.
results.quote:

results.finding: ETS-A transgenic mice: 795 mice analyzed; Syn 0.52 homozygotes developed six digits, including an extra triphalangeal digit.
results.quote: Most Syn 0.52 mice have six digits that are all triphalangeal, but some have seven or even eight digits; this is more severe than the polydactyly seen in the 0.25 ETS-A affinity mice

results.finding: ETS-A transgenic lines: founders crossed to WT generated F1; 795 mice analyzed, with heterozygous and homozygous French 2/Indian 2 mice showing preaxial polydactyly.
results.quote: Heterozygous and homozygous French 2 and Indian 2 mice have preaxial polydactyly in their hindlimbs
